lessons.title: Preparing Tab Ribbons and Flux Application
lessons.body: Tab ribbons are thin strips of tinned copper that connect solar cells together. They come in rolls, usually 2mm wide and 0.15mm thick for standard 5-inch cells. You need to cut them to length: for a 5-inch cell, cut about 12cm for the front and 12cm for the back. Use sharp scissors or wire cutters. Wipe the ribbon with a clean cloth and isopropyl alcohol (or local spirit) to remove oil and dirt. Then apply flux. Flux is a chemical that cleans metal and helps solder flow. You can use rosin flux paste or liquid flux. Apply a thin layer with a small brush or cotton swab. Too much flux leaves sticky residue; too little means solder won't stick. In Africa, where humidity and dust are common, keep flux covered when not in use. Work on a clean, flat surface like a wooden board or ceramic tile. Wear safety glasses and gloves. Good preparation prevents weak joints later. Practice cutting and fluxing 10 ribbons before soldering. A common mistake is touching the ribbon with bare fingers after cleaningâoils from your skin ruin the flux. Always hold ribbons with tweezers or clean gloves. Store cut ribbons in a dry container. If you are using lead-free solder, use a flux designed for it; leaded solder works with rosin flux. Never mix fluxes. For best results, flux both the ribbon and the cell's contact pads. Let the flux dry for 30 seconds before soldering. This step takes patience but ensures strong electrical connections.

lessons.title: Soldering Tab Ribbons to Solar Cell Front Contacts
lessons.body: The front of a solar cell has thin silver lines called fingers and wider busbars. You will solder the tab ribbon across the busbar. Set your soldering iron to 350Â°C for leaded solder or 380Â°C for lead-free. Use a chisel tip, about 3mm wide. Place the cell on a heat-resistant mat. Align the ribbon along the busbar, leaving about 5mm overhang at each end. Hold the ribbon with one hand using tweezers, and the iron with the other. Touch the iron to the ribbon and busbar together for 2 seconds, then feed a small amount of solder (0.5mm diameter) into the joint. Do not press hardâlet the heat do the work. Move the iron slowly along the busbar, soldering in 2cm sections. You should see the solder turn shiny and flow smoothly. If it looks dull or lumpy, you are moving too fast or the iron is too cold. After soldering, inspect the joint: it should be smooth and concave. Let the cell cool for 1 minute before handling. In dusty workshops, cover the cell to prevent contamination. Practice on broken cells first. A good solder joint has low resistance and will not overheat. Remember, solar cells are fragileâtoo much heat cracks them. If you hear a crack, stop and replace the cell. Keep your iron tip clean by wiping it on a damp sponge every few joints. This ensures good heat transfer.

lessons.title: Soldering Bus Ribbons to Solar Cell Back Contacts
lessons.body: The back of a solar cell has a full aluminum or silver coating, often with solder pads. You will solder wider bus ribbons (usually 4mm to 5mm wide) to these pads. These ribbons carry higher current, so they must be thick. Cut bus ribbons to length, about 15cm for a 5-inch cell. Clean and flux the back pads just like the front. Set your iron to the same temperature as before. Place the bus ribbon on the pad, leaving 1cm overhang. Solder from one end to the other, pressing gently. Use a larger solder wire (1mm) for faster melting. The back of the cell is more robust than the front, but still avoid excessive heat. Solder in 3cm sections, allowing 5 seconds between sections to let the cell cool. You should see a bright, smooth solder fillet along the entire ribbon. If the solder balls up, add a little flux and reheat. After soldering, check for bridges between adjacent padsâthey cause short circuits. Use a multimeter to test continuity. In Africa, where power may be unstable, use a temperature-controlled iron; a simple iron can overheat. Practice on scrap cells. A good back solder joint will not peel off when you tug gently on the ribbon. Let the cell cool completely before flipping it over. Store soldered cells in a dry place. Never solder in a windy areaâthe solder will cool too fast and create cold joints.

lessons.title: Using a Soldering Iron with Temperature Control
lessons.body: A temperature-controlled soldering iron is essential for solar panel assembly. Unlike a simple plug-in iron, it lets you set the exact temperature. For solar cells, use 350Â°C for leaded solder (63/37 tin-lead) and 380Â°C for lead-free solder (SAC305). Higher temperatures damage cells; lower temperatures cause cold joints. Buy a station with a digital display, like a Hakko FX-888D or a Chinese equivalent. In Africa, where voltage fluctuates, use a surge protector or a voltage stabilizer. Always let the iron heat up for 5 minutes before use. Clean the tip with a damp sponge or brass wool before each joint. Tin the tip by melting a small amount of solder on itâthis protects the tip and improves heat transfer. When soldering, hold the iron like a pen, at a 45-degree angle. Do not drag the tip; lift it straight up after each joint. If the tip becomes black or pitted, replace it. A good tip lasts about 3 months with daily use. Use a stand to rest the iron safely. Never leave it unattended. After work, turn off the iron and let it cool before storing. For field work, consider a battery-powered iron like the TS100, which runs on 24V. It reaches 400Â°C and is portable. But for workshop use, a station is better. Calibrate your iron every month using a thermocouple. If you don't have a thermometer, test on a scrap cell: if solder melts in 2 seconds, the temperature is right. Keep your workspace well-ventilated to avoid inhaling flux fumes.

lessons.title: Inspecting Solder Joints for Quality
lessons.body: After soldering, inspect every joint. A good solder joint is shiny, smooth, and concave (like a small fillet). It should look like a tiny volcano. A bad joint is dull, lumpy, or ball-shaped. Use a magnifying glass (10x) or a smartphone camera zoom. Check for cracks, which look like thin dark lines. Also look for bridgesâsolder connecting two busbars that should be separate. Use a multimeter in continuity mode to test for shorts. For each cell, measure the resistance between the front busbar and the back pad. It should be less than 0.1 ohms. If higher, re-solder. Tug gently on the ribbon with tweezers; it should not move. If it lifts, the joint is cold. Cold joints happen when the iron is too cold or you move the ribbon before the solder solidifies. In dusty environments, cover the cell after inspection. Keep a log of each cell's resistance. In a 60-cell panel, one bad joint can reduce output by 10%. So inspect all 60. Use a bright LED light to see reflections. A good joint reflects light evenly. Practice by making 10 joints and grading them: 1 (bad) to 5 (perfect). Aim for 4 or 5. If you find a bad joint, mark it with a marker and repair it later. Never ignore a suspicious joint. In Africa, where panels face harsh sun and heat, weak joints fail faster. So quality inspection is critical. After inspection, store cells in a clean, dry box.

lessons.title: Repairing Cold or Weak Solder Joints
lessons.body: Cold joints look dull and grainy. They have high resistance and will overheat. To repair, first clean the joint with isopropyl alcohol. Apply fresh flux. Set your iron to 350Â°C (leaded) or 380Â°C (lead-free). Touch the iron to the joint and reheat for 2-3 seconds. Add a tiny amount of fresh solder. The old solder should melt and blend. Remove the iron and let it cool naturallyâdo not blow on it. If the joint still looks bad, remove all old solder with a desoldering pump or solder wick. Then re-solder from scratch. For a weak joint where the ribbon lifts, you may need to add more solder. Hold the ribbon down with tweezers while soldering. If the cell itself is cracked, the joint cannot be repairedâreplace the cell. After repair, re-inspect and test resistance. It should be less than 0.1 ohms. If not, repeat. In Africa, where replacement cells may be scarce, repair is a valuable skill. Practice on scrap cells. Keep a repair kit: flux, solder, wick, pump, and extra ribbons. Never use acid flux for repairsâit corrodes. Use rosin flux only. If you repair a joint more than twice, discard the cell. Too much heat damages the cell's internal connections. After repair, let the cell cool for 5 minutes before handling. Store repaired cells separately and label them. A well-repaired joint is as good as new. But prevention is better: use correct temperature and clean tips from the start.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Tab Ribbon Soldering Techniques for Solar Panel Assembly

In African solar assembly workshops â from Nairobi's Industrial Area to Lagos's Ikeja and Accra's Spintex Road â tab ribbon soldering is where margins are made or lost. A single cold joint on a 72-cell module can cut output by 0.5â1.5 W, and across a 500-module monthly run that is real money. This reference gives technicians and workshop owners the practical numbers, temperatures, and inspection criteria needed to solder consistently, reduce rework, and protect warranty claims.

Tab ribbons are tinned copper strips (typically 0.15â0.25 mm thick, 1.5â2.0 mm wide) that carry current from cell front contacts to the bus ribbon and onward to the junction box. Soldering quality depends on four variables: iron tip temperature, contact time, flux activity, and ribbon/cell cleanliness. Get these right and you get strong, low-resistance joints. Get them wrong and you get cold joints, micro-cracks, or cell breakage.

Why this matters commercially

In African markets, most solar assembly businesses compete on price, delivery speed, and warranty confidence. A workshop in Kampala or Lusaka that delivers modules with verified solder joints can charge a 5â10% premium and win tenders that require IEC 61215 compliance. Conversely, a workshop that ships modules with cold joints faces returns, reputation damage, and lost repeat business. Soldering is not just a technical step â it is a quality control gate that protects revenue.

Data Table 1: Recommended Soldering Parameters

Parameter SnPb (63/37) SnAgCu (SAC305) Notes
Iron tip temperature 330â350 Â°C 350â370 Â°C Higher for lead-free
Contact time per joint 2â3 s 2â4 s Longer causes cell micro-cracks
Flux type Rosin mildly activated (RMA) No-clean or water-soluble Must be compatible with ribbon
Tip geometry Chisel 3â5 mm Chisel 3â5 mm Flat contact spreads heat
Ribbon thickness 0.15â0.20 mm 0.15â0.25 mm Thicker needs more heat
Peak joint temperature ~183 Â°C (eutectic) ~217â220 Â°C Ribbon must reach this

Sources: IPC-A-610H Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies (IPC, 2020); IEC 61215-2:2021 Terrestrial photovoltaic modules â Test procedures; manufacturer datasheets for SAC305 and SnPb solders.

Data Table 2: Solder Joint Defects, Causes, and Fixes

Defect Visual sign Root cause Corrective action
Cold joint Dull, grainy, uneven surface Insufficient heat or short contact Increase tip temp 10â20 Â°C; extend contact 1 s
Insufficient solder Thin fillet, visible gap Too little solder or flux Add small amount of solder; re-flux
Solder bridge Solder connecting two busbars Excess solder or drag motion Remove with wick; re-solder carefully
Cell micro-crack Hairline fracture near busbar Excessive heat or pressure Scrap cell; retrain technique
Lifted busbar Silver contact detached Overheating or mechanical stress Scrap cell; check iron tip pressure
Flux residue Sticky brown film No-clean flux not cured Clean with IPA; verify flux type

Sources: IPC-A-610H (2020); NREL Technical Report NREL/TP-5200-62364, Photovoltaic Module Reliability (2014); manufacturer field guides for tab ribbon soldering.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Soldering Iron and Fume Hazards

  • Burn risk: Soldering iron tips reach 330â370 Â°C. Never touch the tip or the ribbon immediately after soldering. Use heat-resistant gloves and a proper stand.
  • Fume risk: Flux fumes contain rosin and aldehydes. In African workshops with limited ventilation, always use a fume extractor or work near an open window with a fan. Prolonged exposure causes respiratory irritation.
  • Lead exposure (SnPb solder): Wash hands thoroughly after handling leaded solder. Never eat or drink at the soldering bench. Keep solder away from children.
  • Fire risk: Keep a dry powder or COâ extinguisher within 3 meters of the soldering station. Never leave a hot iron unattended.
  • Electrical risk: Use a grounded, temperature-controlled iron with an RCD/earth leakage breaker. In areas with unstable grid power, add a surge protector.

Step-by-step practical procedure

1. Preparing tab ribbons and flux application. Cut tab ribbon to length (typically 2Ã cell width plus 10 mm overhang). Clean ribbon with isopropyl alcohol (IPA) to remove oxidation. Apply a thin, even layer of flux to the cell busbar using a flux pen or small brush. Do not flood â excess flux causes splatter and residue.

2. Soldering tab ribbons to front contacts. Place the ribbon over the silver busbar. Press the iron tip flat against the ribbon for 2â3 seconds, feeding a small amount of solder at the tip-ribbon interface. The solder should flow smoothly and form a concave fillet. Lift the iron straight up â do not drag.

3. Soldering bus ribbons to back contacts. Flip the cell carefully using a vacuum pen or soft tweezer. Align bus ribbon with back contact pads. Solder in the same manner, ensuring full wetting across the pad. Keep the cell flat to avoid stress cracks.

4. Using a temperature-controlled iron. Set the station to 330â350 Â°C for SnPb or 350â370 Â°C for SAC305. Verify with a tip thermometer weekly. Use a chisel tip (3â5 mm) for best heat transfer. Replace oxidized or pitted tips â they cause cold joints.

5. Inspecting solder joints. Under good light (500â1000 lux) and a 5Ã magnifier, check each joint for: shiny surface, concave fillet, complete wetting, no bridges, no cracks. A good joint looks like a smooth silver ramp between ribbon and busbar.

6. Repairing cold or weak joints. Re-flux the joint, apply the iron for 1â2 seconds to reflow, and add a small amount of fresh solder. Do not overheat â if the joint does not reflow cleanly on the second attempt, scrap the cell. Repeated heating damages the silver contact and the silicon.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Iron tip temperature verified at 330â370 Â°C (depending on solder alloy).
  2. Ribbon and busbar cleaned with IPA before soldering.
  3. Flux applied thinly and evenly â no flooding.
  4. Contact time per joint kept to 2â4 seconds.
  5. Joint appears shiny, concave, and fully wetted.
  6. No solder bridges, cracks, or lifted busbars.
  7. Cell handled with vacuum pen or soft tweezer to avoid micro-cracks.
  8. Fume extractor or ventilation active; PPE worn; hands washed after leaded solder.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • IEC 61215-2:2021 â Terrestrial photovoltaic (PV) modules â Design qualification and type approval â Part 2: Test procedures (International Electrotechnical Commission).
  • IPC-A-610H â Acceptability of Electronic Assemblies (IPC, 2020) â free table of contents and summary; full standard available for purchase.
  • NREL/TP-5200-62364 â Photovoltaic Module Reliability (National Renewable Energy Laboratory, 2014).
  • U.S. Department of Energy â Solar Energy Technologies Office: PV Manufacturing Resources.
  • IRENA â Solar PV Manufacturing and Skills Development Reports (International Renewable Energy Agency).

This module is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills programme. Practical parameters should be validated against the specific ribbon, flux, and cell datasheets used in your workshop. For training enquiries, contact your local RISE AFRICA partner.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of flux when soldering tab ribbons?
options: A) To glue the ribbon to the cell
B) To clean metal and help solder flow
C) To cool the soldering iron
quiz.explanation: Flux removes oxides and reduces surface tension, allowing solder to flow smoothly.

quiz.q: What width of tab ribbon is typically used for standard 5-inch solar cells?
quiz.explanation: Standard tab ribbons for 5-inch cells are about 2mm wide.

quiz.q: After cleaning a ribbon with isopropyl alcohol, why should you avoid touching it with bare fingers?
options: B) Oils from skin contaminate the surface
quiz.explanation: Skin oils prevent flux and solder from adhering properly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended soldering iron temperature for leaded solder?
quiz.explanation: Leaded solder (63/37) melts well at 350Â°C for solar cell work.

quiz.q: When soldering the front contacts, how long should you touch the iron to the ribbon and busbar before feeding solder?
quiz.explanation: About 2 seconds allows the joint to reach soldering temperature without overheating the cell.

quiz.q: What should a good solder joint look like?
quiz.explanation: A quality joint is shiny, smooth, and concave (fillet shape).

quiz.q: Why is it important to let a solar cell cool for 1 minute after soldering?
options: A) To let the flux dry
B) To prevent cracking from thermal stress
C) To allow solder to harden
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling or handling can cause micro-cracks in the fragile cell.

quiz.q: What is the typical width of bus ribbons used for back contacts?
quiz.explanation: Bus ribbons are wider (4-5mm) to carry higher current.

quiz.q: When soldering back contacts, why should you avoid bridges between pads?
quiz.explanation: Bridges create electrical shorts, reducing panel performance.

quiz.q: What tool can be used to test for continuity after soldering?
quiz.explanation: A multimeter in continuity mode checks for shorts and proper connections.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature for lead-free solder?
quiz.explanation: Lead-free solder (SAC305) typically requires about 380Â°C.

quiz.q: Why should you use a surge protector with a soldering station in Africa?
options: B) To protect against voltage fluctuations
quiz.explanation: Voltage spikes can damage the station's electronics.

quiz.q: How often should you clean the soldering iron tip?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning before each joint ensures good heat transfer and prevents contamination.

quiz.q: What is tinning the soldering iron tip?
options: A) Coating the tip with solder
C) Dipping the tip in flux
D) Wrapping the tip in wire
quiz.explanation: Tinning protects the tip from oxidation and improves heat transfer.

quiz.q: What is a cold solder joint?
options: A) A joint soldered at low temperature
B) A joint with too much solder
C) A joint that is dull and high resistance
D) A joint that is shiny and smooth
quiz.explanation: Cold joints occur from insufficient heat or movement, resulting in poor electrical contact.

quiz.q: What resistance value indicates a good solder joint?
quiz.explanation: A good joint has very low resistance, typically under 0.1 ohms.

quiz.q: How can you check if a ribbon is securely soldered?
options: C) Tap it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: A gentle tug reveals if the joint is weak or cold.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a bridge between two busbars?
options: B) Remove excess solder with a wick or pump
quiz.explanation: Removing the bridge eliminates the short circuit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep flux covered when not in use?
options: A) To prevent evaporation and contamination
B) To make it last longer
quiz.explanation: Flux absorbs moisture and dust, which reduces effectiveness.

quiz.q: What is the first step in repairing a cold joint?
options: C) Heat with a hot air gun
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes contaminants before re-soldering.

quiz.q: When repairing a joint, why should you not blow on it to cool it?
options: A) It causes a cold joint
quiz.explanation: Blowing causes uneven cooling and can create a cold joint.

quiz.q: How many times can you safely re-solder a joint before discarding the cell?
quiz.explanation: Excessive heat from repeated soldering damages the cell.

quiz.q: What type of flux should never be used for solar cell repairs?
quiz.explanation: Acid flux corrodes metal and is not for electronics.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when storing soldered cells?
options: B) Keep in a dry, clean box
quiz.explanation: Dry storage prevents corrosion and contamination.

quiz.q: What can happen if you use too much flux?
quiz.explanation: Excess flux leaves residue that can attract dust and cause issues.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a chisel tip on a soldering iron?
options: B) For dragging solder along busbars
quiz.explanation: A chisel tip provides a wide contact area for efficient heat transfer along busbars.

quiz.q: Why should you solder in sections when working on a solar cell?
options: B) To prevent overheating the cell
C) To make it look neat
quiz.explanation: Soldering in sections allows the cell to cool, reducing thermal stress.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overhang for tab ribbons on the front of a cell?
quiz.explanation: About 5mm overhang allows for connection to the next cell.

quiz.q: What should you do if you hear a cracking sound while soldering?
options: B) Stop and replace the cell
quiz.explanation: Cracking indicates the cell is damaged and will not function properly.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use a temperature-controlled soldering iron?
options: B) To maintain consistent temperature for quality joints
C) To make the iron last longer
quiz.explanation: Consistent temperature prevents cold joints and cell damage.
